titleEn: Come and see the works of God
progression: | G G | C D | Em C | G D |
intro: Twenty verses that open by summoning the whole earth and close with one person paying a private debt. Verses 1 to 12 speak as a we: a nation tested, refined like silver, brought through fire and water. From verse 13 the voice is singular and walks into the house with animals in hand. Nothing marks that seam except the number of the verbs and the suffixes, so the grammar is the argument. The line in verse 12, we came through fire and through water, is still ordinary Hebrew for having survived something.

stichs.en: For the leader. A song, a psalm.
Shout to God, all the earth.

verses.summary: The heading names two musical genres before the psalm says anything, and then the first command goes to the whole earth rather than to Israel. The scope is set wide on purpose.

stichs.en: Sing the glory of His name;
make His praise glorious.

verses.summary: Two imperatives in parallel, both aimed at the name rather than at God directly. Praise is handled as an object that can be given weight.

stichs.en: Say to God: how awesome are Your deeds!
Through the greatness of Your strength Your enemies come cringing to You.

verses.summary: The praise is put into the mouth of the singer as direct speech, and the first thing it contains is fear rather than affection.

stichs.en: All the earth bows down to You
and sings praise to You;
they sing praise to Your name. Selah.

verses.summary: Universal homage answers the universal summons of verse 1, and three verbs of bowing and singing close the opening frame.

stichs.en: Come and see the works of God,
awesome in what He does toward the children of man.

verses.summary: A second pair of imperatives, come and see, moves the psalm from sound to sight and sets up the historical evidence.

stichs.en: He turned the sea into dry land;
they crossed the river on foot.
There let us rejoice in Him.

verses.summary: The evidence is a crossing: sea turned to land, river crossed on foot. Then the verb jumps to the present, and a past event becomes an occasion for rejoicing now.

stichs.en: He rules by His might forever;
His eyes keep watch on the nations.
Let the rebellious not exalt themselves. Selah.

verses.summary: The lesson drawn from history is surveillance rather than comfort. The same power that opened the sea is described watching the nations.

stichs.en: Bless our God, O peoples,
and let the sound of His praise be heard.

verses.summary: The peoples are addressed again, and what is asked of them is not belief but noise: their voice is to carry the praise.

stichs.en: who has kept our soul among the living,
and has not let our foot slip.

verses.summary: Two participial clauses give the reason for the blessing. Being kept among the living and being kept from slipping are one act described twice.

stichs.en: For You have tested us, O God;
You have refined us as silver is refined.

verses.summary: The reason turns into an admission. The keeping included testing, and the image of refining makes the suffering purposeful rather than hostile.

stichs.en: You brought us into the trap;
You laid a crushing weight on our loins.

verses.summary: Two blunt clauses with God as the subject of the harm. The psalm does not hand the trouble off to an enemy.

stichs.en: You let men ride over our head;
we went through fire and through water,
and You brought us out to abundance.

verses.summary: The lowest point and the turn in one verse. Fire and water are the two extremes, and the last word means saturation, the exact opposite of the constraint two lines earlier.

stichs.en: I will come into Your house with burnt offerings;
I will pay You my vows.

verses.summary: The plural stops here. From this verse to the end there is one speaker, one house, and one debt being settled.

stichs.en: the vows my lips opened wide to utter,
and my mouth spoke when I was in distress.

verses.summary: The vow is dated backwards to the moment of fear, which is what makes it binding now that the fear is over.

stichs.en: Burnt offerings of fatlings I will offer up to You,
with the smoke of rams;
I will prepare cattle with he-goats. Selah.

verses.summary: The inventory is deliberately expensive. Naming each animal is how the psalm shows a vow being paid rather than merely described.

stichs.en: Come and hear,
and let me tell, all you who fear God,
what He did for my soul.

verses.summary: The private thanksgiving turns public again. The audience narrows to those who fear God, and the subject narrows to one soul.

stichs.en: To Him I called with my mouth,
and high praise was under my tongue.

verses.summary: The testimony is reduced to two organs, mouth and tongue, which keeps the report verbal rather than sacrificial.

stichs.en: Had I looked on wrongdoing in my heart,
the Lord would not have listened.

verses.summary: A condition is admitted that could have voided the whole thanksgiving. The psalm protects its own claim by naming what would have blocked it.

stichs.en: But in truth God heard;
He attended to the voice of my prayer.

verses.summary: The condition of the previous verse is answered flatly. Two verbs of hearing, one general and one attentive, are stacked to say that the prayer landed.

stichs.en: Blessed be God,
who has not turned away my prayer,
nor His kindness from me.

verses.summary: The closing blessing is built as a double negative: nothing was withdrawn. Prayer and covenant kindness are treated as one thing that stayed in place.

pardes.body: Two psalms joined at verse 13. The first half is public and plural: the earth is told to shout, the crossing of the sea is offered as evidence, and the we of the nation reports being tested, netted, ridden over, and brought out. The second half is private and singular: one person walks into the house with animals and pays what he promised while he was frightened. Nothing in the Hebrew marks the seam except the number of the verbs, which is why {{13.0}} is the word to slow down on. The order matters. The nation is delivered first, then one member of it settles the account.

Three words carry real ambiguity. {{11.1}} is either a stronghold or a hunting net, since the noun is attested in both senses, and translations split on this verse; the surrounding language of weight and constraint favours the net, but the reading is disputed. {{17.3}} can be read as a verb, He was extolled, or as a noun, high praise, sitting under the tongue like something held in the mouth, and old versions differ. {{3.7}} literally means they lie or they deny, and is usually rendered cringe or feign obedience, which is the psalm saying that submission under overwhelming force is not the same thing as loyalty.

The image in {{10.3}}, refined as silver is refined, is the psalm's own reading of its history: the trouble in verses 11 and 12 is neither punishment nor accident but process, and the proof offered is that it ended in saturation rather than in loss. Read that way, the first half is a set of instructions for how to speak about a disaster once it is over. {{18.0}} then cuts the other way in the second half: the speaker admits that a prayer can fail, and puts the fault inside the one praying rather than in the one listening. The blessing at the end is therefore not automatic. It says only that this time nothing was turned away, which carries weight because the previous verse allowed that it could have been.

Read as an inner map, the two halves are two stages of one person. The first is the self as a crowd: many voices, public history, events that happen to a group and can be told as a story. The second is the self as a single speaker who owes something and goes to pay it alone, with the mouth as the instrument. Fire and water in {{12.4}} are the standard pair for the two ways a soul comes undone, by burning and by drowning, and coming out to saturation rather than to dryness is how the psalm says the trial gave more than it took. The refining of silver in {{10.3}} makes the same claim from the other side: the metal is not replaced, only the dross leaves.
